text: A simple rain gauge works by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing the water into a cylindrical measuring tube. For accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. If the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch. However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; the collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source of error is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops right over the opening, which causes the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.
